Structure-loss paper · urban conflagration definition

Defining an urban conflagration · 2026-10-13

Updated 13 October, evening: an urban conflagration as a part of a fire (every patch, house-to-house and house-and-tree kinds, a wide set of candidate measures, within-fire tests of what made a patch vulnerable, illustrated explainers). How the working rule (a fire is an urban conflagration when at least 50 destroyed buildings form one connected patch, each within 30 m of the next) was reached and tested on three full records: 358 fires in the USGS Carlson record (2002–2022), 633 in our full 2002–2026 record and 276 CAL FIRE-inspected incidents (2013–2025), each with at least one building destroyed; plus Lahaina 2023 and Waldo Canyon 2012 as outside checks. Every distance and size from 5 to 100 m and 10 to 1,000 buildings, tests for a natural break, published distances, and 6 definitions scored head to head.

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · 2026-10-13 17:01 PDT

New (13 October, evening): an urban conflagration is better treated as a part of a fire. In our full record 6 of the 10 fires with one hold two or more, and at 30 m links most of their destroyed buildings sit outside any patch of 50. Two kinds, defined the same way, are now on the page: house-to-house (destroyed buildings 30 m or less apart) and house-and-tree (up to 60 m apart with trees all the way between); the house-and-tree kind meets the bar we set in advance. Of the many conditions tested within the same fire, only log block size and share on ridges or upper slopes separated blocks that became urban conflagrations from those that did not, with 9 fires carrying the comparison, so most answers are "can't tell". The earlier work follows below.

Short answer: the data do not single out a better definition, and they draw no natural line of their own. The size of the largest connected patch of destroyed buildings rises smoothly from one fire to the next, with no gap that separates town fires from the rest. Destroyed buildings cluster more than chance over a range of link distances, about 20–50 m between building centres, not at one distance. The working rule (30 m links, at least 50 buildings) sits inside that range, and it counts every fire in the CAL FIRE inspections that published reports call an urban conflagration (4 of 4). But it is a knife-edge choice: nudging either number swaps borderline fires in or out, and it misses 4 smaller or more spread-out fires that some reports describe as house-to-house fires (Angora, Chimney Tops 2, Grass Valley, Witch). None of the 5 alternatives did better. We suggest keeping the rule as a stated convention and always reporting which fires are firmly in and which are borderline.

How to read this page

Hover or tap any number, cell, line or point for what it means; switch to Technical at the top for methods and statistics. “Patch” always means: destroyed buildings linked hop by hop, each within the link distance of at least one other in the patch.

New · An urban conflagration as a part of a fire

Added 2026-10-13 (evening, Pacific time). The owner asked: should an urban conflagration describe a whole fire, or a part of one? A fire can hold several separate patches where fire spread from building to building, and those patches can be of different kinds. This section reframes the question around patches and tests much more than distance and count.

Words used on this page

Urban conflagration
On this page: at least 50 destroyed buildings in one connected patch, each within 30 m (centre to centre) of another destroyed building in the patch. A fire can hold none, one or several. (Earlier pages applied it to whole fires: a fire "had" one if its largest patch reached 50.)
Patch
Destroyed buildings joined hop by hop: each within the link distance of at least one other in the patch. A chain, not a circle.
Block of closely spaced buildings
Buildings standing before the fire, inside the area it reached, joined hop by hop when about 20 m or less separate their walls (35 m between centres).
House link / tree link
House link: two destroyed buildings 30 m or less apart. Tree link: up to 60 m apart with pre-fire tree canopy all the way between them.
Buildings the fire reached
Buildings standing before the fire inside its mapped area (earlier pages called these "exposed").

What we have tested so far, step by step

Each step asked one question and was set up before we looked at the answer. Badges: holds = the finding stood up; can't tell = the data cannot decide; didn't help = tested and no improvement; now = this page's new work.Result notes in docs/ledger.d (hover a badge for the file).

  1. 1
    12 Oct Which fires become urban conflagrations? holds
    The size of the biggest block of closely spaced buildings sorts them: in our full record no fire whose biggest block had 89 or fewer buildings had one; above that line, 10 of 24 fires did.
  2. 2
    13 Oct Other ways to describe the loss holds
    Six other measures (share of destroyed buildings with a destroyed neighbour, loss per km², how deep the loss went into town, …) agree, but fires form one continuous spread, not a separate class.
  3. 3
    13 Oct Is the rule (30 m, 50 buildings) natural? can't tell
    No natural size or distance falls out of the data; destroyed buildings hang together more than chance between about 20 and 50 m. The rule is a stated convention, and a knife-edge one.
  4. 4
    13 Oct Is 89 buildings a tipping point? can't tell
    We cannot tell a sharp step from a steep rise: the chance climbs from about 5% to about 50% as the block grows from about 70 to 200 buildings.
  5. 5
    13 Oct Do trees, fences or wind explain which big blocks became urban conflagrations? didn't help
    No. Trees matter in a different kind of loss (Gatlinburg: sparse, wooded housing). No usable fence data.
  6. 6
    13 Oct Only buildings inside the U.S. holds
    Removing buildings across the border changed no fire's outcome; the headline held.
  7. 7
    Now A part of a fire, not the whole fire now
    Patches of destroyed buildings, two kinds (house-to-house and house-and-tree), every candidate measure, and what made a patch vulnerable within the same fire. Results below.

The ideas in pictures

Illustrations only: icons and distances are drawn, not real buildings. Hover any piece for what it means.

A block of closely spaced buildings

Buildings with gaps of about 20 m or less between walls chain into one block; a wider gap starts a new block.

One connected patch of destroyed buildings

Destroyed buildings each within 30 m of another form a patch. An urban conflagration is a patch of 50 or more.

A chain, not a circle

A patch can snake through a neighbourhood; only hops between neighbours count.

Biggest block or all blocks

Earlier we used only the biggest block; this study also counts every block.

House links and tree links

Two ways destroyed buildings can be linked: close together, or further apart with trees all the way between.

New · One fire, many patches

Added 2026-10-13 (evening, Pacific time). Why only the biggest block, the owner asked, when a fire can have several? Here are all of them.

At 30 m a burned town splits into street-sized pieces

Each dot is a building in a 6 km square of the town that burned. At 30 m links Tubbs has 7 separate patches of 50 or more, and its largest holds only 3% of the fire's 5,185 destroyed buildings; Camp (Paradise) has 12, the largest holding 0.6% of 16,493. Streets, yards and parks wider than 30 m cut the burned area into pieces. Switch to 50 or 75 m and the pieces join: at 75 m Camp's largest patch holds 61%. So the old rule, which looked only at the largest patch, saw a fragment of each of these fires.maps.parquet (p31a): Carlson points (public domain) in a 6 km square centred on the fire's largest 30 m patch; patch membership computed on all of the fire's destroyed buildings; colours = patches ≥ 50 at the chosen link distance, ordered by size.

All three records: half or more of these fires hold two or more urban conflagrations

Using every patch cannot change which fires count (a fire has a patch of 50 exactly when its largest patch is 50 or more). It changes how many urban conflagrations a fire has and how much of its loss they hold. On the side of the buildings standing before the fire, counting all blocks instead of the biggest one predicts which fires have an urban conflagration no better: our full record 0.994 vs 0.995 (difference +0.001, 95% range -0.004 to +0.006). New · Two kinds: house-to-house and house-and-tree

Added 2026-10-13 (evening, Pacific time). The owner asked for a definition that includes trees and houses together, and for both kinds to be defined well.

Two kinds of urban conflagration, defined the same way

Both kinds use the same rule: at least 50 destroyed buildings in one connected patch. They differ only in the link. House-to-house: destroyed buildings within 30 m of each other. House-and-tree: destroyed buildings up to 60 m apart with tree canopy (at least a quarter of the ground, on the tree map from two years before the fire) all the way between them. A patch can be both; a fire can hold several kinds. Named Carlson fires: Camp 2018: 1 house-to-house, 31 house-and-tree, 3 both, 5 mixed chain; Tubbs 2017: 7 house-to-house, 3 house-and-tree, 1 mixed chain; Almeda Drive 2020: 7 house-to-house, 1 house-and-tree, 1 both, 2 mixed chain; Sayre 2008: 4 house-to-house; Valley 2015: 3 house-and-tree, 1 mixed chain; Marshall 2021: 4 mixed chain. One fire dominates the tree kind: 31 of the 43 house-and-tree patches in the Carlson record are in Camp (Paradise), a wooded town.Tree canopy: USFS Science Tree Canopy Cover, ignition year − 2 (PA36 leak rule); tree link = every 10 m sample along the segment ≥ 25 % (10 m skipped next to each building). Kind of a combined patch (house or tree links, ≥ 50) from h / t = share of its members in a house-only / tree-only patch ≥ 50; ≥ 0.5 decides.

How this panel was checked
  • Three full records; Lahaina has no tree map (outside the continental U.S.).
  • The tree map is from two years before each fire, so it cannot see the fire.
  • 30 m canopy pixels are coarser than a gap between houses; the rule asks for canopy along the whole line, sampled every 10 m.

How each kind scores against published descriptions

The house-and-tree kind meets the bar we set in advance (stable in all three records, no more spread-out losses counted than the house kind, and it counts Gatlinburg): well defined. Combining both links counts the published town fires at least as well as the house rule and is more stable, but by the pre-set rule it is not clearly better (can't tell).Scorecard as PA34 (p31_scorecard.csv); stability = mean Jaccard over N ×/÷ 1.5, link distance one step, tree reach 50 / 75 m, canopy 17 / 38 %; tree-kind bar: stability ≥ 0.6 in all three records, W flagged ≤ house kind, Gatlinburg called. Decision vs A0 for A7: can't tell.

New · What made a patch vulnerable, within the same fire

Added 2026-10-13 (evening, Pacific time). Comparing blocks of closely spaced buildings inside the same fire removes everything that differs between fires (weather, firefighting, fire size). Which blocks became urban conflagrations?

What separates blocks that became urban conflagrations from blocks that did not

Each row is something measured on a block of closely spaced buildings before the fire. We compare blocks inside the same fire, of the same size. In our full record 9 fires had both a block that became an urban conflagration and one that did not (CA_2008_SAYRE, CA_2017_TUBBS, CA_2018_CAMP, CA_2018_WOOLSEY, CA_2020_GLASS, CO_2021_MARSHALL, DINS_2025_EATON, DINS_2025_PALISADES, OR_2020_ALMEDA_DRIVE); they carry the comparison, so only large, consistent differences can show. Consistent in at least two records: log block size, share on ridges or upper slopes. Carlson's fires are also in our full record, so agreement between those two is not independent; the CAL FIRE inspections are the independent check. Block size is partly built in (a bigger block has more buildings that can make up 50). The ridge result is fragile: only 7% of these blocks have any building on a ridge or upper slope, and CAL FIRE does not show it. Rows marked * are fire weather or wildland fire, shown for description only.Conditional logit with fire strata (house-to-house, house-and-tree) and fire fixed-effects regression on logit(destroyed share); predictors standardised within record; each adjusted for log block size; fire-cluster bootstrap 2,000; Holm within record and outcome over V1–V11 (+V7b, V7c); 'holds' = Holm p < 0.05 in ≥ 2 records with the same sign.

New · Houses, trees and wind

Added 2026-10-13 (evening, Pacific time). Three things the owner suggested may set a patch off: how close the houses are, how much tree canopy links them, and the wind when the town burned.

Houses × trees, coloured by what happened; wind in the small charts

Each dot is a block of 50 or more closely spaced buildings that a fire reached (442 blocks, three records combined). Right = bigger block; up = more trees between the houses. House-to-house urban conflagrations sit to the right whatever the trees; house-and-tree ones reach higher up, in more wooded blocks. Wind-driven patches: described, not defined

Fire weather is never part of the definition (it would describe the weather, not what burned). We describe each patch instead: the wind, and two signs of ember-driven spread around it. 1 · The working definition and where it came from

An urban conflagration is a wildfire that turns into a town fire, spreading from building to building. To study them we needed a rule that says, from a map of destroyed buildings, which fires did that.

What the rule counts

A patch grows hop by hop. Each destroyed building joins the patch if it is within 30 m (centre to centre) of any destroyed building already in it. So a patch is a chain through a neighbourhood, not a circle. The fire's size as an urban conflagration is the number of buildings in its largest patch.Largest single-linkage cluster of destroyed building centroids at linkage L (LDC_L); working definition LDC_30 ≥ 50. Equivalent to connected components of the graph joining destroyed pairs ≤ L apart.

How this panel was checked
  • Illustration only: the six buildings are drawn, not real; distances printed in the hovers are those of the drawing.

Two real fires, four link distances

In Tubbs 2017 fire spread house to house through Santa Rosa's Coffey Park; Chimney Tops 2 2016 destroyed about as many buildings in and around Gatlinburg, spread over steep, wooded hills. Switch the link distance. At 30 m, Tubbs passes the 50-building line (143) and Gatlinburg does not (16), but even Coffey Park, which burned almost completely, is split into many patches. At 50 m they join into one of 1,250; at 100 m Gatlinburg's largest patch reaches 500. The answer depends on the distance chosen.USGS Carlson points (public domain), 2.4 km square centred on each fire's largest 30 m cluster; colour = membership of the fire-wide largest cluster at L (computed on all the fire's destroyed points, not just the window).

How this panel was checked
  • Points are the USGS Carlson record (public domain); no coordinates beyond metres within the square are published.
  • The largest patch is computed on the whole fire; the square only shows part of it, and the hover gives the count inside the square.
  • The two fires were picked before looking at their patch sizes beyond 30 m: Tubbs as a fire everyone calls an urban conflagration, Chimney Tops 2 as a large but spread-out loss (both in the earlier analysis).

How we got to the working rule

  1. 8 October 2026. While checking whether our model finds the same big-loss fires as the labels, we needed a yes/no for “this fire became an urban fire”. The project lead suggested: a connected patch of at least 50 destroyed buildings with 30 m links. We reported 25 and 100 buildings and 50 m links alongside, and noted then that 30 m splits Paradise (Camp Fire), whose houses sit about 26 m apart.
  2. 12 October. We asked which fires reach that line. The best single predictor was the size of the largest block of closely spaced buildings the fire reached (about 20 m between walls): no fire below about 89 such buildings reached 50 destroyed in one patch. The chance rose steeply but smoothly, with no step.
  3. 13 October, morning. Six other ways of describing the loss (share of destroyed buildings with a destroyed neighbour, loss per square kilometre, how deep the loss went into town, and others) all separate these fires from the rest, but they form one continuous spread, not a separate class of fire.
  4. 13 October, this page. The rule itself was chosen, not derived. Here we test it.

2 · The space of possible definitions

A rule of this kind has two numbers: how close two destroyed buildings must be to count as linked, and how many linked buildings make a conflagration. We tried every combination on a grid.

3 · Does a natural break fall out of the data?

A definition is most defensible when the data draw the line themselves: a size where fires split into two groups, or a distance at which fire spread typically links buildings.

Is there a natural size? The largest patch, fire by fire

If urban conflagrations were a separate kind of fire, the curves would drop and then flatten, leaving a gap between ordinary fires and town fires. They don't: patch sizes thin out smoothly from 1 building to over a hundred. A formal test for a second peak found none at any distance from 5 to 100 m in any record (smallest unadjusted p = 0.12). The 50-building line sits on a smooth slope; it is a convention.Complementary CDF of LDC_30 over fires with n_dest ≥ 10. Silverman critical-bandwidth test (2,000 smoothed bootstraps) on log10 LDC_L, 10 L × 3 records, Holm-adjusted p ≥ 1.00 everywhere (min raw 0.117). Fisher–Jenks 2-class break at 30 m: 8 [5–11], 8 [5–11], 7 [6–16] buildings (bootstrap CI spans more than a factor 2); Gaussian mixtures prefer 2 components at L ≥ 20 m, but on skewed data that is expected and not separation (PA33).

USGS Carlson record, 2002–2022Our full record, 2002–2026CAL FIRE inspections, 2013–202550-building line
Share of fires with a patch at least this big (log scale)
How this panel was checked
  • Fires with at least 10 destroyed buildings in each record (so a patch of 1 is not counted just because only 1 burned).
  • Patch sizes are whole numbers; the test adds a random half-building jitter so ties do not make false peaks.
  • Holm correction over the 30 tests named before the run; the bar needed a significant result at the same distance in two records.
  • The 2-component mixture result is reported but not used as evidence of a gap: mixtures always split skewed data.

Is there a natural distance? How the largest patch grows as the link distance grows

As the link distance grows, more destroyed buildings join the largest patch. If house-to-house spread had one typical range, the curves would jump at the same distance in every fire. They don't. Half of a fire's destroyed buildings are in one patch by 320 m for Almeda Drive, 68 m for the Camp Fire (Paradise, larger lots), 191 m for Tubbs and 235 m for Gatlinburg; the typical fire rises gradually over the whole range.f(L) = LDC_L / n_dest on 61 log-spaced L (exact, from the minimum spanning tree), median and IQR over fires with n_dest ≥ 50; named fires dashed.

Share of the fire's destroyed buildings in its largest patch
How this panel was checked
  • Fires with at least 50 destroyed buildings; the band shows the middle half of fires.
  • Lahaina is drawn as a curve of shares only (BRIGHT labels, CC BY-SA 4.0: aggregates only).
  • Use the key to hide lines.

Destroyed buildings cluster more than chance, building up between about 20 and 50 m

For each fire we redrew the same number of destroyed buildings at random among the fire's own buildings, and compared the largest patch. Real patches are bigger than chance at every distance above 5 m. Half of the extra clustering is reached by 20 m between centres and nearly all of it by 50 m; beyond that it adds little (in the CAL FIRE inspections it falls again). So the distances at which destroyed buildings hang together more than chance span roughly 20–50 m, and 30 m sits inside that range. Fire by fire, the distance of strongest clustering varies by more than a factor of two, so the data give a range, not one number.Contagion ratio = LDC_L / mean of 50 random-labelling draws, median over fires with n_dest ≥ 20, fire-bootstrap 95 % CI. Pre-registered bar for a natural linkage distance (per-fire IQR < ×2 and medians within ±25 % in all three records) not met for L_jump or L_contag; L* kept at 30 m. The levelling-off distance is exploratory (not in the prereg).

  • The chance comparison keeps each fire's own buildings and its number destroyed, so it controls for town layout and fire size; it cannot separate house-to-house spread from the fire front reaching one neighbourhood and not another.
  • Intervals come from resampling fires.

  • Wall-to-wall gaps use equal-area circles from building footprints; footprints were found for under half of destroyed buildings (rest take the fire's typical size). On Lahaina, where real outlines exist, the circles underestimate how connected buildings are (the 30 m centre patch matches a ~10 m true wall gap).

4 · What physics and published work say

A good definition should agree with what is known about how fire jumps between buildings, and with how fire scientists describe these events.

Published definitions and distances

No published source gives a number that defines an urban conflagration in a wildfire; the definitions are in words (building-to-building spread that overwhelms firefighting), or a count of homes lost. The distances that recur are gaps between buildings at which one burning building ignites the next: 1.8–40 m wall to wall, most often 9.1–18 m. For typical houses (about 13 m across) that is roughly 22–31 m between centres, which overlaps the range where our destroyed buildings cluster beyond chance.Literature search 2026-10-13 (WebSearch/WebFetch), each reference verified by DOI or official URL; distances converted to the grid as wall gap (edge-gap grid) or centre distance.

5 · 6 definitions, head to head

We scored the working rule against 5 alternatives on criteria fixed before any score was computed.

6 candidate definitions

A is the working rule. B to F are the 5 alternatives; their thresholds were set by splitting each measure where it divides most cleanly in our full record, without looking at which fires are famous. (A version of A with a distance and size taken from the data was planned too, but the data gave no such distance or size, so it is the same as A.)Thresholds: Fisher–Jenks 2-class break on R2 fires with n_dest ≥ 10 (log scale for counts, densities and areas); L* = 30 m (no natural linkage distance (bar not met): current 30 m kept); N* = 50.

DefinitionNeeds
AWorking rule: At least 50 destroyed buildings in one patch with 30 m linksonly the destroyed buildings' locations
BAt least 26 buildings destroyed per km² of built-up land the fire reacheddestroyed buildings plus a map of all buildings (developed area)
CAt least 41% of destroyed buildings have another destroyed building within 30 monly the destroyed buildings' locations
DA connected destroyed area (30 m links) of at least 0.4 hectaresonly the destroyed buildings' locations
EAt least 83 buildings destroyed in the fire (count only)only the destroyed buildings' locations
FAt least 50 destroyed buildings in one patch with 30 m links and at least 26 buildings destroyed per km² of built-up land the fire reacheddestroyed buildings plus a map of all buildings (developed area)

  • The list is not a random sample: it over-represents famous California fires, and the 'not building-to-building' list is shorter on official detail.

6 · Recommendation and what it would change

What the evidence supports, and how the list of fires and the exposure line change.

What we conclude

What the pre-set test says: we can't tell which definition is best. None of the 5 alternatives matched the published descriptions at least as well as the working rule while also being more stable or cleaner at its line, and the working rule itself does not sit on a stable plateau. Searching the whole grid for the best match to the published list (after the fact) picks 75 m links and at least 200 buildings, but chosen fairly (leaving each named fire out in turn) it matches no better than the working rule (0.70 vs 0.80 on our full record), so that is noise, not a better rule.

What we suggest for the paper. Keep “at least 50 destroyed buildings in one patch, each within 30 m (centre to centre) of the next” as a stated convention, and say why it is reasonable: 30 m between centres picks the same fires as about 15–20 m between walls for typical houses (estimated from building size; in Lahaina, where real outlines exist, it corresponds to about 10 m), inside the 9.1–18 m separations most often cited for house-to-house ignition, and inside the range where destroyed buildings cluster beyond chance. Always report the fires that qualify under every nearby rule (the core: Almeda Drive 2020, Eaton 2025, Palisades 2025, Sayre 2008, Tubbs 2017) separately from the borderline ones, and give the 50 m version as a sensitivity.

Worth testing next. A companion analysis that also links destroyed buildings up to 60 m apart when continuous tree cover lies between them turns Gatlinburg's largest patch from 16 buildings into 326, matching the report that calls it an urban conflagration, while Black Forest (7 → 11) and Bastrop (5 → 13) stay scattered. That idea, links through fuel as well as distance, was not part of the test fixed in advance here, so it is a candidate for the next round, not a result.

Does the 89-building line move?

Earlier we found that no fire whose largest block of closely spaced buildings held 89 or fewer met the working rule. That result holds only for the 30 m rule: with 50 m links, 12 fires in our full record with blocks of 89 or fewer count, and the line drops to about 21 buildings. Part of that line is built in. A 30 m patch of destroyed buildings lies inside one block of closely spaced buildings, so the block is at least as big as the patch in 99.7%, 99.7%, 100.0% of fires: no fire can count below about 50 by construction. The real evidence for 89 is that none of the 15, 16, 13 fires with blocks of 50–89 buildings counted (with so few fires, the true rate there could still be as high as 22%, 21%, 25%, exact 95% upper limits).Two-rate cut (m4) on log10(1 + largest exposed component, 35 m centroid links) with 2,000 fire-bootstrap resamples, fires with ≥ 100 exposed (PA31 eligibility). Mechanical bound: share of fires with b20 ≥ LDC30 (p28_mechanical_bound.csv). The separate PA35 check found the climb gradual (about 5% at 60–70 to 50% at 190–210 buildings).
